newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola reappoints prime minister for new unity govt.
newsitem.headline: Angola reappoints prime minister for new unity govt.

text.p: Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos dissolved his cabinet on Wednesday as one of the final steps to forming a new power-sharing government, state television announced.
The country is scheduled to get a government of national unity on Friday, after many postponements, delays and a shaky peace treaty signed after two decades of civil war in 1994.

Dos Santos also issued a decree reappointing Fernando Franca Van Dunem as prime minister to head the new "Unity and National Reconciliation Government", which will include members of the former rebel UNITA movement.
Ministers in the dissolved cabinet will keep their positions in a caretaker capacity until Friday's inauguration ceremony, to be attended by several heads of state.

Earlier this week parliament rushed through a bill which gave UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi special status as president of the largest opposition party. The law gives him, among other things, the right to regular consultation with the national president and an official residence in Luanda.

Seventy UNITA deputies, who won their parliamentary seats in the aborted elections of 1992, were sworn in on Wednesday, but Savimbi has said he will not be travelling to Luanda to participate in Friday's ceremony.
He says the security situation is not stable enough for him to leave his Bailundo headquarters in Angola's central highlands.

Four UNITA members are set to become ministers and the party will also have seven deputy-ministerial positions and a number of ambassadorial posts, but diplomats said they did not expect dos Santos to make major cabinet changes.

"There will not be any big reshuffle, certainly not in the immediate future," said one diplomat. "I expect almost everyone, except those positions to be occupied by incoming UNITA people, will be reappointed."
Portugal's President Jorge Sampaio arrived in Luanda on Wednesday night and South African President Nelson Mandela was expected at the ceremony in the newly repainted parliamentary building.
The United Nations, which has started a gradual withdrawal of its 6,000-strong peacekeeping force, believes the inauguration is a crucial step in implementing the 1994 Lusaka Protocol.
That agreement officially ended the war between UNITA and the MPLA government which erupted on independence from Portugal in 1975.
Political analysts are divided over the significance of the new government and to what extent it can consolidate peace in Angola.
